reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
clinicalPearls: An uncommon surface-epithelial ovarian tumour composed of nests of transitional-type (urothelium-like) epithelium set in a dense fibrous stroma
The overwhelming majority are benign, small, solid, and discovered incidentally in middle-aged or older women
Frequently unilateral and often coexists with a mucinous cystadenoma in the same ovary
The epithelial nests may show longitudinal nuclear grooves, giving a coffee-bean appearance, and are thought to derive from Walthard cell rests of transitional metaplasia
Coarse calcification within a solid ovarian mass on imaging is a helpful pointer
Borderline and malignant variants exist but are rare; malignant Brenner tumours behave as transitional-type carcinomas
Occasionally the stroma is hormonally active and produces oestrogen, causing postmenopausal bleeding or endometrial hyperplasia
reference.pathophysiology: Brenner tumours are surface-epithelial-stromal neoplasms in which islands of transitional-type epithelium, resembling urothelium, are embedded in an abundant fibromatous stroma. The epithelium is believed to originate from metaplastic transitional cells, analogous to the Walthard cell nests found near the tubo-ovarian junction. In benign lesions the nests are well circumscribed with bland, grooved nuclei and frequent central cystic change or mucinous metaplasia, which explains the common association with mucinous cystadenomas. Malignant transformation, when it occurs, produces frankly invasive transitional-cell carcinoma. Some tumours have a hormonally active stroma capable of oestrogen secretion, accounting for occasional endometrial effects.
additionalDifferentials: Transitional-cell (urothelial-type) carcinoma metastatic from the urinary tract
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound showing a solid, often calcified ovarian mass
Pelvic MRI or CT to characterise a solid lesion and detect coexisting cysts
Tumour markers (CA125 and others) mainly to exclude malignant or metastatic disease
Endometrial assessment if oestrogenic effects such as postmenopausal bleeding are present
Histology with immunohistochemistry to confirm transitional-type epithelium and grade the lesion
Urinary tract imaging or cystoscopy if a metastatic urothelial carcinoma is considered
redFlags: A solid ovarian mass with rapid growth or solid enhancing components suggesting a malignant variant
Postmenopausal bleeding indicating oestrogenic stromal activity requiring endometrial evaluation
Ascites or peritoneal disease pointing to a malignant or metastatic process
reference.prognosis: Benign Brenner tumours are cured by simple excision with an excellent outlook. Borderline lesions rarely recur, whereas malignant Brenner tumours carry a prognosis comparable to other invasive ovarian carcinomas and depend on stage at diagnosis.
pitfalls: Confusing a solid, calcified Brenner tumour with a fibroma or malignant ovarian mass on imaging
Overlooking a coexisting mucinous cystadenoma in the same ovary
Failing to investigate oestrogenic symptoms such as postmenopausal bleeding
Assuming all transitional-type epithelium is benign and missing a malignant variant
references: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
management: Treat benign tumours with surgical excision, typically unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, with ovarian cystectomy considered in younger women wishing to preserve fertility
Manage borderline and malignant Brenner tumours with cytoreductive staging surgery including hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, and omentectomy as for ovarian carcinoma
Add platinum-based chemotherapy for malignant transitional-type carcinoma according to stage
Confirm the diagnosis histologically with immunohistochemistry and assess for a coexisting mucinous cystadenoma in the same ovary
Investigate any oestrogenic effect such as postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial assessment
Refer borderline or malignant disease to a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team with stage-based surveillance for recurrence
